summary: Carbimazole is a thionamide antithyroid drug widely used outside the United States (UK/Europe/India); it is a prodrug rapidly converted to methimazole, its active form, which is FDA-approved in the US. It inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis and is used to treat hyperthyroidism (Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter) and to prepare patients for thyroidectomy or radioiodine. Key risks are agranulocytosis (warn patients to report fever/sore throat), hepatotoxicity, and first-trimester teratogenicity.
indications: Hyperthyroidism, including Graves disease and toxic multinodular goiter
Preparation of hyperthyroid patients for thyroidectomy
Control of hyperthyroidism before and after radioactive iodine therapy

dosage.d: 15-40 mg/day (up to 60 mg/day in severe cases), often in divided doses until euthyroid
dosage.n: Carbimazole ~10 mg is roughly equivalent to methimazole ~6 mg

dosage.d: 5-15 mg/day once euthyroid; titrate to thyroid function
dosage.n: Continue typically 12-18 months (titration or block-and-replace regimens)

dosage.d: Initial ~0.5-1 mg/kg/day in divided doses; maintenance titrated down
dosage.n: Adjust to thyroid function and tolerability

dosage.d: Titrate to achieve euthyroid state before the procedure
dosage.n: May be combined with beta-blocker for symptom control

admin: Administer orally; divided dosing initially, often once daily for maintenance
Obtain baseline CBC and liver function before starting
Counsel the patient to stop the drug and seek urgent testing for fever, sore throat, or mouth ulcers (possible agranulocytosis)
Monitor thyroid function and titrate the dose to maintain euthyroidism
moa: Carbimazole is rapidly and almost completely metabolized to methimazole, the active moiety. Methimazole inhibits thyroid peroxidase, blocking the oxidation and organification of iodide and the coupling of iodotyrosines, thereby reducing synthesis of thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). It does not inactivate existing circulating or stored hormone, so clinical response is delayed until hormone stores are depleted.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to carbimazole, methimazole, or product components
Severe pre-existing bone marrow suppression / agranulocytosis from prior thionamide use
relative: First trimester of pregnancy (teratogenic risk - prefer propylthiouracil)
monitor: White blood cell / neutrophil count, especially with fever or infection

preg: Methimazole (carbimazole's active form) crosses the placenta and can cause fetal harm in the first trimester, including aplasia cutis and methimazole embryopathy (choanal/esophageal atresia, omphalocele, facial dysmorphism). Propylthiouracil is generally preferred in the first trimester; if used, employ the lowest effective dose and monitor fetal thyroid function.
lact: Methimazole is excreted in breast milk; at low to moderate maternal doses it is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding while monitoring the infant's thyroid function.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is established; use with caution in renal impairment.
hepatic: Use with caution; thionamides can rarely cause cholestatic or hepatocellular injury. Monitor liver function and discontinue if significant hepatotoxicity occurs.

major: Anticoagulants (warfarin) - restoring euthyroidism alters anticoagulant requirements; risk of altered INR
moderate: Beta-blockers, digoxin, theophylline - clearance changes as thyroid status normalizes (may need dose reduction)
Other myelosuppressive drugs - additive marrow suppression
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; keep timing consistent.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; avoid excess to limit additive hepatic stress.
interactions.diagnostics: Alters thyroid function tests; affects radioiodine uptake studies (discontinue before radioiodine as directed).

serious: Agranulocytosis (sudden severe neutropenia - fever, sore throat)

monitoring: Full blood count (especially neutrophils) at baseline and if infection/fever occurs
Liver function tests at baseline and as clinically indicated
Thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4) periodically to guide dosing
Symptoms/signs of vasculitis with long-term therapy
counsel: Stop the medicine and get an urgent blood count if you develop fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, or signs of infection (possible low white cells)
Report yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine, or severe abdominal pain (liver problems)
It may take several weeks to feel the full effect as existing hormone is used up
Do not stop suddenly without medical advice; keep regular blood-test appointments
If pregnant or planning pregnancy, tell your doctor - the drug is avoided in early pregnancy
pk: Clinical effect delayed days to weeks (until hormone stores deplete)
Active methimazole peaks within ~1-2 hours of conversion
Methimazole half-life approximately 4-6 hours (intrathyroidal action longer)
Antithyroid effect persists well beyond plasma half-life; often once-daily dosing
Store below 25 C (77 F); protect from light and moisture
pearls: NOTE: Carbimazole is not FDA-approved in the US; its active metabolite methimazole IS FDA-approved - prescribing data below are sourced from the methimazole label plus EMA/BNF references
Carbimazole is a prodrug rapidly converted to methimazole (~10 mg carbimazole ~ 6 mg methimazole)
Warn every patient about agranulocytosis - stop and check FBC for fever/sore throat
Avoid in the first trimester (teratogenic embryopathy); propylthiouracil preferred early in pregnancy
Response is delayed because the drug blocks synthesis, not release of stored hormone; a beta-blocker controls symptoms meanwhile
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and continue the regular schedule. Do not double the dose.
overdose: Acute overdose may cause nausea, vomiting, headache, and, with large or chronic excess, bone marrow suppression (agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia) and hypothyroidism with goiter. Management is supportive: gastric decontamination if recent and substantial, monitor blood counts and thyroid function, and treat marrow suppression/infection. There is no specific antidote.
